Investment memo · Nexans (NEX-FR) · 5 November 2026

Nexans: contracted earnings growth to 2028 at a trough multiple, with consensus estimates likely to fall in February 2027 before the July 2027 results can lift the shares

Price €113.60 (23 Oct 2026)Market cap €5.1bnEV €6.6bnPhase: BottomingNext event: 24 Feb 2027
The bottom line for Richard

Nexans offers a return of about 23 percent over 14 months at its own ten-year median multiple, against about 10 percent downside to a trough multiple on unchanged earnings: a skew of roughly 2.5 to 1 in the shareholder's favour. The return comes from contracted earnings growth and dividends, not from a re-rating.

Two dated events set the timing. The FY2026 results on 24 February 2027 will probably cut consensus EPS and cash estimates and bring a light first FY2027 guide. The H1 2027 results in late July 2027 are where Nexans can prove its Transmission margin and raise guidance.

The practical stance is to build a position across the February event rather than ahead of it. A signed replacement order for the Halden plant before February would be the signal to act sooner.

0Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

Nexans is now a pure electrification cable maker with three engines of very different quality. The exit from every other business was completed on 3 July 2026. Transmission makes and lays high-voltage subsea and land cable systems. Grid supplies medium-voltage cable and accessories to distribution utilities. Connect sells low-voltage cable for buildings, industry and data centres, and now includes Republic Wire in the United States.

The investment case is earnings growth that is largely contracted, bought at a trough multiple. Viewforth's model takes adjusted EBITDA from about €805m in FY2026 (the guidance midpoint) to €909m in FY2027 and €1,013m in FY2028. EPS rises about 26 percent in FY2027 and 19 percent in FY2028, from a FY2026 that is flat on a continuing basis. About four-fifths of the FY2027 EBITDA increase is already contracted, acquired or mechanical: Transmission contracts priced in 2023 to 2026 replace legacy contracts, the new Electra cable-laying vessel replaces chartered vessels, Republic Wire contributes a full year, and new Grid capacity adds volume.

The share price already discounts a great deal of bad news. The shares trade at 10.4x consensus two-year-forward earnings, the 5th percentile of five years, after a 24 percent fall in six months. Half of that fall reflects the sector's de-rating. The other half reflects four pieces of company news: the revenue hole left by the halted Great Sea Interconnector project, an acquisition (Republic Wire) at 10x EBITDA, a miss on Transmission volume, and a replacement order that has not yet been signed.

The return comes mostly from delivery, not from re-rating. To 31 December 2027 (14 months), the total shareholder return is about +23 percent at the stock's ten-year median multiple of 12.3x: earnings contribute about 16 points, dividends about 6 points and the multiple roughly nothing. At 11.05x, the guideline multiple for a stock in the Bottoming phase, the return is about +11 percent. At the 15.82x used in the model summary it is about +57 percent; 15.82x is a peak-delivery multiple, so I treat that return as the bull case, not the base case.

The six things that matter most, in order of importance.

1. Consensus estimates must fall a little before the multiple can rise a lot, and both events are dated. The sell-side has the operating story right (segment margins, Grid, the replacement order) and the financial story wrong. Consensus EPS sits 5 to 10 percent above what the accounts will support, for three reasons: the brokers' EPS basis excludes amortisation of acquired intangibles and uses basic shares; consensus depreciation cannot be reconciled with the depreciation reported for H1 2026; and consensus uses a tax rate of 27 to 29 percent against a reported 31 to 33 percent. Consensus FY2027 free cash flow of €439m is far above any estimate that includes leases, reorganisation cash and a flat backlog.

The FY2026 results in February 2027 will therefore probably cut FY2027 EPS estimates by 3 to 6 percent and FY2027 cash estimates by 15 to 25 percent. By habit, Nexans will probably set its first FY2027 EBITDA guide 2 to 4 percent below the €936m consensus median. The H1 2027 results in July 2027 are where a guidance raise becomes likely (45 to 50 percent), provided the replacement order is signed and the H1 Transmission margin prints at 15 percent or better. The sequence is: cut, absorb, prove, re-rate.

2. The one binary item, the replacement Halden order, is more likely to resolve well than the market's anxiety implies; its timing is the real risk. Nexans has been preferred bidder since July 2026 for a replacement mass-impregnated cable order to load its Halden plant in Norway; engineering is under way, and Deutsche Bank expects the award by late 2026. Part of the market misread the Mallorca-Menorca award of 22 October as this order, but the Mallorca-Menorca link uses extruded cable. Across the three European majors, no preferred-bidder position has fallen away in five years, and conversion into a signed contract has taken 9.6 months on average, which points to signature by late April 2027 at the latest. I put the probability of losing the order outright below 10 percent and the probability of signature after end-March 2027 at about 35 percent. Each quarter of delay costs €5m to €8m of EBITDA; each half-year with the Halden line idle costs €15m to €20m net.

3. Grid is the engine that both the company and the sell-side under-model, and it offers the cleanest positive skew in the case. Grid grew 14.8 percent organically in Q3 2026 against 6 to 7 percent expected. Two-thirds of Grid revenue sits under six- and seven-year frameworks (Enedis doubled its annual volumes), and Nexans will add 40 percent more European cable capacity and 39 percent more accessories capacity by 2028 into a market where demand exceeds supply. The company guides to mid-single-digit growth, the model has 8 to 9 percent, and consensus FY2027 Grid EBITDA (€248m) sits below the model's €255m. Grid can surprise upwards every quarter, and it is the one segment the company discloses quarterly.

4. Nexans is the weakest of the three European high-voltage leaders; the caveat is real but bounded. Nexans has the thinnest high-voltage backlog (€7.8bn against NKT's €13.0bn and Prysmian's €16.5bn plus €2bn awarded), has lost 3 to 4 points of European subsea share, has added the least capacity, and runs a Transmission margin 650 to 750 basis points below its two peers. Its distinctive asset, Halden's mass-impregnated cable line, uses a technology the market is slowly leaving. The model therefore closes only about half the margin gap (to 16.6 percent by FY2028) and holds Transmission flat after mid-2028. The compensation is that Transmission is 28 percent of Nexans's EBITDA, against 75 percent at NKT, so a post-2029 debate about high-voltage capacity reaching parity with demand hurts Nexans least of the three.

5. Cash lags earnings throughout the forecast period, and the 2028 cash-conversion target is the target Nexans is most likely to miss. Free cash flow converts about 30 to 40 percent of EBITDA to 2028, against 47 percent in 2025 and a company target above 45 percent on a full basis. Three forces hold cash conversion down: capex stays at 4 to 6 percent of sales; the tailwind from customer down-payments has ended because the backlog is flat; and leases, interest, tax and reorganisation cash have all risen. The balance sheet still deleverages to about 0.5x net debt to EBITDA by end-2028 without acquisitions, which creates an unpriced option: a €500m buyback at today's price would add about 7 percent to FY2028 EPS. Management has said it prefers acquisitions, which add about 4 percent to FY2028 EPS for the same money.

6. The cheapness headline is partly a basis effect, so the re-rating case is a return to the median multiple, not to the top of the range. On consensus EPS the stock trades at 10.4x, the 5th percentile of five years. After the February estimate cuts, the same price will read about 11x, the 25th to 35th percentile of ten years; on the model's lower EPS the multiple is already about 12.2x. About half of the apparent 18 percent discount to the ten-year median will therefore close through estimate cuts rather than price rises. The return comes mostly from earnings growth and dividends, with the multiple a modest helper, unless the sector's own regime turns; technical momentum is rated D or F across the whole peer group.

Phase and setup. By the dashboard's rule and in my view, the stock is in the Bottoming phase. The turn up is most likely in July 2027, and possibly in February 2027 if the order is signed first. Of Richard's six setups, the closest is "cause-for-concern clearing in a medium-quality business on a first-quartile multiple, reverting to normal". Three things spoil the fit: Connect's cyclicality; the modest size of the concern (Halden is worth €15m to €25m a year inside about €900m of EBITDA); and a sector regime that explains 57 percent of the stock's daily moves.

1Operating environment: strong, funded tailwinds and bounded headwinds

The structural demand for grid cable is strong, set in law and funded, and it reaches Nexans fastest through Grid and North American Connect. The figure below lists the main forces. Grid grew 14.8 percent organically in Q3 2026, with breadth across European utilities, North American utilities and data centres, South American solar, Turkey and Morocco. Connect, helped by North America, grew 12 percent organically in Q2 2026 and 10.5 percent in Q3. Protectionism helps local producers: the EU Net-Zero Industry Act scores bids on non-price criteria, the US Section 232 tariff on imported copper cable is 50 percent, UK and Dutch operators apply local-content rules, and Enedis chose Nexans on security of supply and carbon as well as on price.

Three forces run the other way, and each is real but bounded.

First, the high-voltage award cycle has entered a slower, more price-sensitive phase. TenneT re-phased 7.7 GW of German offshore connections by up to a year; Elia postponed projects, citing "unprecedented price increases"; Energinet paused connections; and Germany moved its unawarded direct-current corridors back to overhead lines, removing over 4,000 km of potential underground cable from the industry's 2027 to 2032 workload. Prysmian has described an "air pocket" in high-voltage direct-current (HVDC) awards. New entrants have also crossed the 525 kV and vessel barriers: LS Cable won TenneT's BalWin4 and LanWin1 projects; Hellenic Cables qualified at 525 kV in July 2026 and won €2.65bn of work from IPTO, the Greek transmission operator and Nexans's Great Sea Interconnector customer; and Sumitomo opened its Nigg plant in September. Nexans's backlog has been flat at €7.7bn to €7.8bn for nine months.

Second, European construction contracted for a 53rd consecutive month in September 2026. Rexel's Q3 showed France soft and the Nordics still struggling, and no broker expects a European residential recovery before 2028.

Third, non-metal input costs rose after the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. European gas is above €90 per MWh, polymer prices are at multi-year highs and bunker fuel is up about 100 percent. Nexans buys energy at least 18 months ahead, so the higher energy cost reaches its accounts mostly in 2027. Prysmian's Q3 already showed a three-month lag in passing polymer costs through to its Power Grid margin.

The macro regime hurts the multiple more than the earnings. The US ten-year yield is near 5.1 percent, Brent crude is about $111 and French sovereign spreads are at decade highs, but all of Nexans's debt is fixed-rate.

Inference: the environment helps each engine differently. The structural tailwind reaches Nexans most powerfully in Grid, the segment with the shortest cycle and the best disclosure. In Transmission, the segment with the highest margins, the tailwind has matured into a question of converting the backlog into profit and replacing it. In Connect Europe, the segment with the lowest barriers to entry, the headwind is bounded. Metal prices affect revenue and working capital, not profit: 83 to 85 percent of sales are indexed to metal prices, and record copper prices inflated FY2026 revenue at current metal prices by about 17 points with no effect on adjusted profit. Polymers, energy and labour are not indexed, however, and the 2010 precedent (about €70m of EBITDA lost on a 25 percent rise in polymer prices) is the right size of worry for 2027.

So what: the environment supports the earnings path to 2028 but not Transmission volume beyond the signed backlog. The environment supports the model's Grid growth above the company's own guideline, and it supports the Transmission margin gains through 2028 on contracts already priced. It argues for a Connect margin below 12 percent in FY2027 (the model has 11.8 percent), with about €20m of net input-cost drag.

Counter-case. The strongest counter-case is that the high-voltage "air pocket" turns into a pricing round for post-2029 delivery slots in which newly qualified bidders undercut the incumbents, bringing the plateau in Transmission margins forward to 2028. The first evidence will be the prices at which the 525 kV awards now being contested clear, and NKT's Q3 commentary on 19 November 2026. What would change my view: a quarter of Grid organic growth below 5 percent, which would signal a capacity or demand problem, or Rexel's European volume turning negative again.

Versus the market. The sell-side knows all of these facts but under-weights two of them. Grid's strength is structural rather than seasonal: management is adding 39 percent more accessories capacity because demand outruns supply. And the roll-off of Nexans's energy hedges lands in H2 2027, which no broker quantifies for Nexans.

Conclusion: The tailwinds are strong, structural and arriving fastest in Grid; the high-voltage business has shifted from a volume story to a conversion story; and European construction and non-metal input costs are real but bounded headwinds. The environment therefore supports the earnings path to 2028 without supporting Transmission volume beyond it.

Score: 72, set by the Rater. Funded forces set in law (EU Grids Package EUR 530-540bn, TenneT EUR 65bn, US transmission and distribution capex, data-centre orders, local-content and tariff protection) reach Grid (+14.8% organic in Q3) and North American Connect, and the 2023-26 high-voltage price regime is locked in the backlog to 2028. Against them sit the high-voltage award air pocket with new 525 kV entrants, a 53-month European construction contraction and unindexed input costs landing in 2027; consensus sales growth at the 77th percentile fits a strong but offset positive. I sit above the group's 66 because the funded grid demand reaches most of the business as it now is, but below RELX because Transmission volume beyond the backlog and Connect Europe are not supported.

2Internally driven corporate change: the self-help is done and the execution programme lies ahead

The transformation that made Nexans a focused electrification company is finished, and it was large. Nexans sold AmerCable ($280m), Lynxeo (€525m) and Autoelectric (€207m enterprise value, closed on 3 July 2026), and closed its Hanover plant. Its SHIFT programme cut the customer base from 20,000 to 4,000 accounts, delivered about €300m of structural EBITDA and took the group margin from 6.1 percent in 2020 to 11.9 percent in 2025.

The whole top of the company then changed within thirteen months. Julien Hueber, a 23-year insider who took the margin of Grid and Connect Europe from 6.7 to 16.4 percent, replaced Christopher Guérin as chief executive on 13 October 2025; the shares fell nearly 10 percent that day. Vincent Piquet (formerly of Renault Ampere and General Electric) became finance director in January 2026, and Stéphane Artaud (formerly of Saint-Gobain, in industrial performance) became Chief Operating Officer on 1 November 2026. A new executive committee includes heads for data centres, large projects and North America; the North America head, Tim King, came from Southwire's integration team. The board is 80 percent independent, and Quiñenco has cut its stake from 28.8 percent to 4.13 percent and left the board.

The programmes now under way are at the execution stage. The figure below dates them. Three need more detail. The new accessories capacity has already cut US lead times by up to 60 percent. Republic Wire (€680m enterprise value; 10.3x 2027 EBITDA before synergies and 7.6x after €23.6m of synergies) is integrating with synergies "ahead of schedule", and a 30 percent capacity expansion comes online by December 2026. Electra replaces chartered vessels and is booked to end-2028.

The negatives cluster around the same execution load. The replacement order remains unsigned three months after Nexans became preferred bidder, and the Transmission backlog is flat while share is being lost. Net debt, return on capital, cash conversion and the Connect margin have all deteriorated (tiles above). The nine-month release omitted all profit, margin and cash data for the first time. Capital allocation prefers acquisitions at 10x EBITDA to buybacks, with the shares at about 7x EBITDA. The board has not explained three credibility items: €781k of shares sold by the outgoing chief executive and finance director before they left, a waived presence condition on 31,794 performance shares, and the absence of a clawback.

Inference: the change forces are broad and coherent, but their character has changed. The forces are bound to the 2028 targets through the chief executive's incentives and are well resourced for the organic programmes. But they have moved from completed, self-financed self-help that could surprise upwards to dated, contracted, execution-stage programmes. A team that is new at every level runs them, and that team has thinned its disclosure just when investors need proof.

The best evidence for the new team is its first year: it protected guidance through the loss of the Great Sea Interconnector, beat H1 2026 by 7 percent, found a replacement order at preferred-bidder stage within a quarter, and delivered Grid growth from the division the chief executive built. The worst evidence is that the delivery record the market relies on belongs to executives who left on terms the board has not explained.

So what: the internal forces justify the Transmission margin step and Grid volume, but not convergence with peers. I have reasonable confidence in the Transmission margin step, because the roll-off of old contract vintages and Electra's arrival are mechanical, and in Grid volume on new capacity. I have less confidence in Republic Wire's synergies and in the Connect margin recovery. The internal forces do not justify convergence to peers' margins, nor the 2028 ambition without acquisitions.

Counter-case. The strongest counter-case is organisational overload: a new chief executive, finance director and Chief Operating Officer, five new regional heads and a US platform bedding in while several capacity ramps run at once. Overload of that kind is the condition under which this company's past crises (2013, 2018) arrived. What would change my view: a second Republic Wire-sized deal at a similar multiple (negative), or a buyback beyond anti-dilution (positive, and a signal that the board has heard the arithmetic).

Versus the market. The sell-side treats the leadership change as succession risk and the acquisitions as positive. I give more weight to two other facts. The Chief Operating Officer's appointment is an admission that industrial execution is the binding constraint, and he would lead any consolidation of Connect Europe's plant footprint, which I put at 30 percent probability of announcement by the FY2027 results. The October disclosure regression removes investors' ability to tell "fine and quiet" from "slipping and quiet" until February.

Conclusion: The corporate change forces are broad, coherent and adequately resourced, but they have moved from proven self-help to execution-stage programmes under a wholly new team. They support margin and volume gains to 2028, while the proof, and the capital-allocation choice, still lie ahead.

Score: 62, set by the Rater. Large dated internal moves with a clear earnings effect to 2028: Republic Wire (US building-wire entry, about EUR 80m of the EUR 285m EBITDA bridge), Electra replacing chartered vessels, 40% more European Grid and 39% more accessories capacity, and 525 kV production, after a completed SHIFT and perimeter transformation. Offsetting them are a wholly new team, net debt up to EUR 1.0bn, ROCE down to 15%, thinner disclosure, acquisitions at 10x preferred to buybacks and unexplained exit terms. I sit above the group's 56 because the brief counts a new-country acquisition and capacity programmes as large forces whether or not their proof is in yet, but well below NKT, whose change is self-funded and already beating expectations.

3Value chain, industry structure, business model, financial profile and management

High-voltage subsea cable is one of the best industry structures in capital goods. Prysmian, Nexans and NKT hold over 80 percent of European subsea transmission, and only five or six companies outside China can both make and lay extra-high-voltage cable. Prices per kilometre of 525 kV HVDC cable roughly doubled between the 2019 to 2020 and the 2024 to 2026 award vintages. Customers pay 10 to 15 percent down-payments and reservation fees, and all three leaders put margin before volume ("the party is over"; "not disappointed to lose share on the wrong projects"; "we don't want to consume cash for projects which are not accretive").

The other two markets are less attractive. Medium-voltage distribution cable is concentrated nationally and is moving to six- and seven-year frameworks. Low-voltage cable is fragmented in Europe, where powerful distributors (Rexel, Sonepar and Wesco) take 10 to 15 percent mark-ups. In the United States it is a disciplined duopoly: Prysmian (with Encore and now Atkore) and Southwire (with $2bn of modernisation) hold 60 to 65 percent of building wire between them.

The support for high-voltage margins has an end date. Morgan Stanley puts high-voltage supply-demand parity around 2030, with about 15 percent oversupply if European offshore wind is built at 13 GW a year. In the last surplus (2015 to 2020) high-voltage margins fell below 5 percent; Prysmian's fell from 17.9 to 5.7 percent in a year.

Nexans is a member of the top tier, not its leader. It owns the assets that define the tier: three cable-laying vessels including the 13,500-tonne Electra, Halden's mass-impregnated and extruded cable lines, the Charleston plant, four copper-rod mills covering about half its copper needs, and the Lens recycling plant. It is at or near the top in European Grid. But it is one-third of Prysmian's size, has the thinnest backlog of the three and has lost 3 to 4 points of European subsea share. It chose not to build speculative subsea capacity, which is consistent with its 2012 to 2018 experience of about €1bn of capex with negligible return. Its Transmission margin is 13.7 percent against peers' 20 to 21 percent; it lacks the optical fibre needed for the combined offer data centres want; and it entered US building wire with about 4 percent share and Canadian copper rod that tariffs block.

Nexans's distinctive niche is a duopoly in a fading technology. Deep-water mass-impregnated cable is a Nexans-Prysmian duopoly (Prysmian has about twice Nexans's capacity), which gives pricing power on deep Mediterranean links. Extruded cable is slowly displacing the mass-impregnated technology, and the installed bases of the two are expected to be equal by 2030.

Nexans's business model is value over volume. The company culls unprofitable accounts, refuses dilutive work, indexes metal prices fully (with no lag on major contracts), runs working capital near 1 percent of standard sales, and grows by adding capacity in Grid and by acquisition elsewhere. The model maximises returns on existing assets and cedes share in a growing market. Nexans's competitive advantages are real but shared with two peers rather than held over them: they are widening in Grid, stable in high-voltage capability, narrowing in high-voltage share and scale, and absent in low voltage.

The financial profile is good, not great. Return on capital employed (ROCE) was 21.3 percent in 2025, fell to 15.0 percent in H1 2026 after Republic Wire and capacity spending, and recovers to about 18 to 19 percent by 2028 on the model. The 2025 margin on standard sales of 11.9 percent compares with Prysmian's 14.2 percent, NKT's 14.3 percent and Cenergy's 16.9 percent. Cash conversion is good over a cycle but depends on project down-payments. Net debt was 1.4x EBITDA at June 2026 on the company's basis, all debt is fixed-rate, and the credit rating is BB+.

Nexans's reported earnings need cleaning in four places. Reported profit includes gains on the "Core exposure" (the company's permanent metal stock); reorganisation costs recur but are excluded from adjusted EBITDA; €23m of integration costs were capitalised; and the tax rate is 30 to 33 percent.

Management is competent, disciplined and bound to the 2028 targets, but unproven as a team. The incentive plan targets 2028 EBITDA of €1.15bn with a 45 percent cash-conversion floor, plus a relative shareholder return that vests nothing below the Eurostoxx 600 industrials. The ambition is measured and margin-led: 3 to 5 percent organic growth in a market growing 6 to 8 percent, and a 17 percent Transmission margin. The strategy is robust rather than bold; it would hold up in a downturn but would capture less of an extended scarcity window than peers' strategies. The governance framework is prudent (one share, one vote; an 80 percent independent board; capped severance), but discretionary decisions have favoured continuity and growth over returning capital.

Inference and so what: the industry structure supports margins through 2028 and becomes fragile from 2029, more so for Nexans than for its peers. Prices in the backlog are fixed and metal-indexed, which protects margins through 2028. From 2029 the structure is fragile, and more fragile for Nexans because its backlog is shorter, its specialised Halden line uses a fading technology and its US entry sits inside someone else's oligopoly. The mitigant is that Transmission is only 28 percent of EBITDA, so Nexans is the least dependent of the three leaders on high voltage.

Counter-case. The strongest counter-case to "weakest of three" is that the weakest converter also has the most mechanical room to improve. About 450 basis points of the 750 basis-point margin gap comes from legacy contracts, under-absorption at Halden and vessel charter costs, all of which close without any new pricing. European Grid, where Nexans leads, is also the segment with the most demand fixed in law. What would change my view: a 525 kV award lost to an entrant on price in Nexans's home markets (France, Norway, Benelux), or a preference for local supply like IPTO's in Greece spreading to Italy and Spain.

Versus the market. The market explains the discount to peers (about 30 percent on EV/EBITDA) by execution history and business mix. I would add that part of the discount is structural and will not close (scale, backlog depth, no optical fibre), which is why I anchor the fair multiple at the stock's own median rather than at peers' multiples.

Conclusion: Nexans sits inside one of the best industry structures in capital goods, with a robust value-over-volume model, above-average returns and a competent new team. But it is the weakest of the three high-voltage leaders on the measures that decide how much of that structure it captures, so its foundations justify durable returns and a median multiple rather than a premium.

Score: 57, set by the Rater. Qualitatively a member of one of the best structures in capital goods (three players hold over 80% of European subsea high-voltage cable, margin-first behaviour, down-payments) and a leader in framework-backed European Grid, but the weakest of the three high-voltage leaders on backlog, share, capacity and margin (13.7% against 20-21%), with no pricing power in the 40% of EBITDA in Connect, a medium-cyclical history of crises (2013, 2018) and a new team. ROCE of 21% in 2025 (15% in H1 2026) beats the 44th-percentile reported ROIC, but new capital is going into a 10x acquisition, and margin percentiles in the 15th-22nd are distorted by metal pass-through; coherent with the four groups at 52-58.

4Guidance conservatism, expectations management and delivery record

Nexans's pattern is to guide light, raise at the half-year and confirm at nine months. It has met or beaten its first EBITDA guidance in every year since FY2022 (table and chart below), has issued no profit warning since 2018, and met every indicator set at its 2021 capital-markets day.

The 2028 ambition has never been raised. The target of €1,150m plus or minus €75m, which includes "additional M&A", has been reaffirmed three times. Prysmian and NKT have both raised their mid-term targets, and Prysmian is now set to exceed its own two years early.

Management talks above its own formal ranges. Consensus sits about 1.5 percent above the FY2026 midpoint (€817m against €805m). Management says it is "working to deliver better than the midpoint", and Deutsche Bank reports it "targeting the top end". Informal commentary also runs ahead of formal ranges: Transmission margins "will improve in 2026", the 17 percent Transmission margin for 2028 is "fully on track", and Grid is growing "well above" its guideline.

Guidance is unusually specific in its building blocks and silent below EBITDA. The FY2026 guide stated its assumptions: no Great Sea Interconnector, the mass-impregnated line loaded at year-end, Republic Wire from June, and no future acquisitions. The 2028 ambition comes with a bridge by segment, dated capacity plans, and a synergy split with a timetable. But the company guides nothing between EBITDA and EPS and does not define its cash measure.

Inference: Nexans is an honest tracker with a conservative bias, not a sandbagger whose upgrades compound. The one 2026 raise was acquisition-led, and the 2028 figure needs acquisitions. The near-term consequence is asymmetric: the pattern favours the company at half-year events and works against it at full-year events.

  • 24 February 2027. The first FY2027 guide is likely (70 percent) to have a midpoint of about €905m to €920m, 2 to 4 percent below the €936m consensus median. If the replacement order is still unsigned, the company will probably exclude its loading effect, as it excluded the Great Sea Interconnector, which would put the midpoint nearer €880m to €900m (10 percent).
  • Any single event. A guidance reduction is improbable (10 to 15 percent).
  • Late July 2027. A raise of €20m to €40m is close to an even chance (45 to 50 percent), if the order and the H1 Transmission margin arrive.

So what: there is no favourable gap at the February event; the favourable gap is Nexans's July habit. FY2026 will be met at or slightly above the midpoint (my central expectation is €805m to €820m), while the market expects the top end. The mid-term targets split as follows.

Counter-case. The strongest counter-case is that the market has learned to discount the light initial guide; if so, a light guide would fail to reset expectations and would expose the stock to a later miss. The 7 percent fall on 22 October, on a sales beat, suggests the market is discounting an execution gap rather than a sandbag, so I think the light-guide-then-raise pattern still works. What would change my view: a February guide with a midpoint at or above €936m (management breaking its habit, which would mean both the order and the Grid capacity are in hand), or a Connect margin below 11 percent in H2 2026.

Versus the market. Compiled consensus already needs about 140 basis points of H2 Transmission margin improvement (Bernstein), and ratings are at their most bullish in a year: 69 percent Buy, ten of twelve visible broker models at Buy or Overweight, and a mean target price of €168. The market is therefore positioned for a February beat that the company is unlikely to deliver. I expect one or two downgrades and target-price cuts of 5 to 10 percent around February, before the July proofs.

Conclusion: Guidance is conservative, specific and reliably met, but upgrades are infrequent and the only 2026 raise was bought through an acquisition. The February 2027 guide will therefore probably sit below consensus, and the favourable asymmetry is confined to a July 2027 raise that depends on the order and the Transmission margin.

Score: 65, set by the Rater. An honest tracker with a conservative bias: FY2022-FY2026 guidance met or beaten (a 15% beat in FY2024), no profit warning since 2018 and every 2021 capital-markets-day indicator met. But FY2025 landed slightly below the revised midpoint, the only 2026 raise was acquisition-led, the 2028 ambition has never been raised and needs M&A, and consensus already sits above the FY2026 midpoint with the cash-conversion target likely missed. Coherent with the Guidance group's 58 and the Sell-side group's 45, placed just above MITIE because the record against formal guidance is clean.

5Revenue growth into outsized profit growth: pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out and feedback loops

Pricing power is demonstrated in Transmission and Grid and absent in Connect.

In Transmission, the industry's price rise is already in the backlog. About €60m to €75m of the €94m rise in Transmission EBITDA between FY2025 and FY2028 comes from executing contracts priced in 2023 to 2026 in place of legacy, inflation-exposed frameworks that finish by late 2026; Electra's removal of vessel-charter costs adds most of the rest. None of the €94m depends on a new price increase, which is why H1 2026 Transmission EBITDA rose 21 percent on flat sales. The next price signal is slightly negative: Nexans negotiated the replacement mass-impregnated order from a position of urgency (Bernstein's "reduced bargaining power"), and awards for delivery after 2029 clear against more bidders.

In Grid, pricing power works through indexation and mix. Prices are metal-indexed, non-metal inputs are recovered through framework renegotiation with a lag, and accessories, which earn about twice the margin of cable, add about 50 basis points of mix by 2028.

In Connect, there is no real pricing power. The Connect margin fell from 13.6 to 11.8 percent in a year, and distributors reprice weekly. US building-wire prices are set by the duopoly at a tariff-supported level, with more downside than upside: Atkore's margin halved from 30 to 15 percent when supply normalised, and Morgan Stanley's earlier work had US margins at 11 percent by 2028.

Operating leverage is moderate for the group and concentrated in Transmission. On the company's own sensitivity, one point of revenue moves EBITDA by about €11m, an incremental margin of about 18 percent and roughly 1.5 times the average margin. The model's FY2025 to FY2028 incremental EBITDA margin on standard sales is 19.5 percent (€285m on €1,465m), consistent with that sensitivity.

  • Transmission: high. Plants, vessels and the dedicated mass-impregnated line are fixed costs; a half-year with the line idle costs €15m to €20m net.
  • Grid: medium. Capacity and staff arrive ahead of volume, which is why the model holds the Grid margin at 15.8 to 16.0 percent through FY2027 before it reaches 16.4 percent.
  • Connect: low. Costs are largely variable, and the margin moves on mix and unindexed inputs.

The largest new fixed cost is depreciation, which rises from 3.2 percent of standard sales in FY2024 to about 4.3 percent. Higher depreciation keeps EBIT growth below EBITDA growth in FY2026; from FY2027 EBIT grows faster than EBITDA.

Financial leverage is low, fixed-rate and falling, and it explains the flat FY2026 EPS. Net financial items roughly double to about €100m in FY2026, because of acquisition debt, negative carry and a hedging loss. That increase is the main reason FY2026 EPS is flat on a continuing basis while EBITDA rises 11 percent. From FY2027 financial leverage becomes a modest tailwind, as net financial items fall towards €55m by FY2030 (worth about €0.70 of cumulative EPS). The €400m 5.5 percent bond is repaid from cash in April 2028. Each €10m of financial items is worth about €0.16 of EPS.

Cost-out is small. About €60m to €75m of gross efficiencies are identified for 2027 to 2029: Republic Wire synergies of €23.6m, SHIFT AI at about €40m, and the Chief Operating Officer's purchasing and footprint work. About €30m to €40m of that reaches EBITDA after 3 to 4 percent wage inflation and the 2027 rise in energy costs. SHIFT already took the easy overhead savings, and metal costs are passed through rather than saved. The latent lever is Connect Europe's plant footprint, which might yield €20m to €40m a year after two to three years, with restructuring cash spent first.

Two reinforcing loops drive profit to 2028, while two balancing loops already act on cash and orders. The figure below sets out the four loops. From 2029 the balancing loops reach margin. The forecasts embody a trade-off that Nexans's selectivity creates: fewer new awards mean less down-payment cash now, but a smaller margin cliff later than NKT faces.

Inference and so what: revenue growth of about 6 percent a year becomes EBITDA growth of about 12 percent, but the profit growth comes from margin mechanics and is front-loaded. Revenue grows about 5.9 percent a year (about 4.5 percent organic), EBITDA about 11.7 percent a year to FY2028, and EPS about 12 percent a year from FY2025 to FY2030 (26 and 19 percent in FY2027 and FY2028, from a flat FY2026). That is outsized profit growth, but it comes from margin mechanics and the reversal of below-EBITDA drags, not from revenue. After FY2028 no driver of comparable size is visible inside the current perimeter, so the FY2029 to FY2030 EPS path depends on how the balance sheet is used.

Counter-case. The strongest counter-case is that the Transmission margin stalls at 15 percent, because the replacement order was priced in urgency and the mix shifts to land and US work; in that case the largest source of operating leverage halves. What would change my view: an H1 2027 Transmission margin below 15 percent with the Halden line loaded.

Versus the market. The street models the margin path well and the drop-through to EPS badly. The arithmetic that a €500m buyback adds 7 percent to FY2028 EPS, against 4 percent for an acquisition at 9.5x EBITDA, is Viewforth's, not the street's, and the market does not yet price any change in capital allocation.

Conclusion: Revenue growth of about 6 percent a year converts into EBITDA growth of about 12 percent and EPS growth of about 20 percent a year in FY2027 and FY2028, through contracted Transmission pricing, Electra, Grid capacity and falling interest. But the conversion is mechanical and front-loaded, pricing power is absent in the 40 percent of the business that is Connect, and the next leg of growth after 2028 depends on how the balance sheet is used.

Score: 55, set by the Rater. Real operating leverage concentrated in Transmission (fixed plants, vessels and a dedicated line; about 64% incremental margin to FY2028) with pricing power proven only through the scarcity-cycle backlog, medium gearing in Grid, and largely variable costs and no pricing power in Connect. The group incremental margin of about 18-19.5% is only about 1.5x the average, cost-out is small (EUR 30-40m net) and financial leverage is low and falling. The FY2027-28 ratio of EPS growth to revenue growth of about 3x comes from margin mechanics and the reversal of below-EBITDA drags rather than structural gearing, and EPS over FY2025-30 grows about twice as fast as revenue, the median, so this is the ordinary-plus mix of the 50 level, coherent with the groups at 52-54.

By segment, Connect adds the most EBITDA and Transmission adds the most margin. The model takes Transmission EBITDA from about €204m (a 12.4 percent margin) to €298m (16.6 percent) by FY2028 on sales only 9 percent higher. Transmission organic growth is -4, +6 and +7 percent in FY2026 to FY2028 and +2 percent afterwards, and the Transmission margin is flat after mid-2028 because no mass-impregnated work is visible beyond then. Grid EBITDA rises from €218m to €282m on 8 to 9 percent annual growth, with the margin held through the capacity ramp. Connect EBITDA rises from €291m to €413m, of which Republic Wire contributes about €30m in FY2026 (seven months), €72m in FY2027 and €80m in FY2028. Other Activities add about €20m.

Growth to FY2030 matches the last five years' pace but is narrower and more mechanical. Standard sales grow about 5.9 percent a year to FY2030, in line with the last five years' organic pace. But Grid (8 to 9 percent a year) and the Republic Wire acquisition carry that growth, while Transmission grows at a flat to low-single-digit rate and Connect Europe is flat. The margin gains about 170 basis points over five years, against about 580 basis points in 2020 to 2025, so the margin improvement is half the size and more mechanical. EPS growth is double-digit (about 12 percent compound from FY2025 to FY2030) and concentrated in FY2027 and FY2028.

The FY2026 EPS "fall" is a perimeter and basis artefact. Consensus and the model both show FY2026 EPS 10 to 13 percent lower than FY2025. On a continuing, like-for-like basis, however, EPS is flat at about €6.4 on the Analyst's diluted basis, because higher depreciation, higher financial items and a higher tax rate absorb €77m of extra EBITDA.

Two-thirds of the €285m EBITDA rise from FY2025 to FY2028 rests on strengths Nexans has already demonstrated. The demonstrated strengths are the contract vintage, delivered capacity and vessels, Grid demand and European integration; over the next 18 months their share of the rise is nearer four-fifths. The undemonstrated third sits almost entirely in FY2028: US low-voltage pricing against the duopoly, a Connect Europe margin without a construction recovery, Halden's loading after mid-2028, and cash conversion above 45 percent. The chart below splits the bridge by source.

My judgement on the model: I support its operating inputs and lean its EPS slightly lower. Two independent analysts converged on EBITDA within 1 percent from different angles. On EPS, H1 2026 depreciation of €153.4m carried only one month each of Electra and Republic Wire. The FY2026 depreciation run-rate excluding acquired intangibles is therefore nearer €296m than the model's €285m, and FY2027 nearer €315m than €300m, which takes about €0.20 to €0.25 off EPS a year. The figures in this memo are the model's before that input change (see end notes).

On cash, the model is slightly generous against the Analyst but fine against the company's own definition. The model's free cash flow sits €10m to €25m above the Analyst's full-basis cross-check, because the model carries no reorganisation cash. On the company's own definition (before lease principal), FY2026 free cash flow lands near the €280m midpoint of the guided range, which is better than the Analyst's "lower part of the range" reading.

Scenarios: the base case carries 65 percent of the probability, and even the downside case leaves FY2028 EBITDA about 15 percent above FY2026. The cards below give each case's EBITDA, EPS and assumptions. Capital deployment sits on top of every scenario: €0.5bn to €1.3bn of acquisitions at 9 to 10x EBITDA would add €0.40 to €0.90 to FY2028 EPS, and a buyback of similar size would add more.

Versus consensus: EBITDA is close, EPS is 5 to 8 percent lower and free cash flow is far lower. The free-cash-flow difference is my highest-conviction difference, because it rests on arithmetic rather than on operating judgement.

Conclusion: The model gives double-digit EPS growth (about 26 and 19 percent in FY2027 and FY2028) on a margin rising from 11.9 to 13.4 percent, with EBITDA close to consensus and EPS and cash well below it for definitional and below-the-line reasons. I support the model's operating path while leaning its EPS about 2 percent lower for depreciation.

Score: 79, set by the Rater. The 10-15% band gives B; the honest base is the continuing one, because the FY2026 fall is a perimeter and basis artefact. Placed in the lower-middle of the band: the margin rises to 13.4-13.6%, above anything in the past, but about 28% of the EBITDA bridge is bought (Republic Wire), the growth is front-loaded in FY2027-28 and partly a reversal of below-EBITDA drags, and it plateaus after FY2028.

7Scope for upgrades to guidance, sell-side estimates and the narrative over 6 to 12 months

February 2027 is a cut event for the financial lines and a confirmation event for the operating lines. The table below sets out what I expect for each consensus line. The EPS cut comes from the accounts, which will probably show total depreciation of about €310m to €320m against a consensus line of €268m, a tax rate near 31 to 32 percent and the final purchase-price allocation for Republic Wire. The FY2027 free-cash-flow cut comes when the company gives its first FY2027 cash range. Net revision breadth is already negative (FY2027 EPS -3 percent over one month; the dashboard's revision-momentum score down from 7 at end-September to 1) and stays negative through February.

Grid is the one line where a February upgrade is plausible. Consensus FY2027 Grid EBITDA is €248m against the model's €255m, and the Q4 print will probably show double-digit organic growth again.

The H1 2027 results in late July 2027 are where the upgrade scope lies. H1 2027 will be the first clean half-year, free of changes in the perimeter. The Transmission comparison is easy (organic growth of -0.1 percent in H1 2026). On the sector's average conversion time, the order will be signed by April and loading Halden from Q2. Grid capacity will be landing, and Republic Wire will report its first clean half-year. If those conditions hold, Nexans will probably raise its FY2027 range by €20m to €40m (45 to 50 percent), consensus FY2027 EBITDA will move back to €915m to €930m, and consensus EPS to about €8.5 to €8.8 on the brokers' basis.

February itself has only a 20 to 25 percent chance of bringing net upgrades. Net upgrades in February would need three things together: the order signed and disclosed before the results, FY2026 EBITDA of €820m or better with an H2 Transmission margin above 15 percent, and a FY2027 guidance midpoint at or above €930m.

The sell-side knows the segment story but has not written up the three financial dynamics behind most of the EPS and cash gap. Brokers cover Transmission conversion, the order, Grid, Republic Wire and supply-demand parity around 2030. But no broker reconciles brokers'-basis EPS with continuing EPS, only two model the step up in depreciation and tax, and none examines the full-basis definition of the cash target. Only Bernstein has reported that the Mallorca-Menorca link uses extruded cable.

Investor positioning appears light. Investor commentary beyond the brokers is not directly observed. The second-hand evidence (Deutsche Bank's feedback from investor calls and Jefferies's account of "clients' minds") says investors ask about the order, the Transmission margin, Republic Wire's start and the discount to peers. The whole sector's technical rating of D or F also points to light positioning.

Three novel positives are not yet in the narrative.

  • A restart of the Great Sea Interconnector. Surveys resumed on 26 October; Meridiam holds 66 percent of the project; the chief executive targets a 2028 restart of production; and the Cypriot regulator has moved completion to January 2031. I put the probability of a binding restart decision inside 18 months at about 30 percent.
  • Data-centre awards for superconducting or 800-volt direct-current cable from the gigawatt-scale quoting pipeline.
  • Any move towards buybacks.

A 2027 capital-markets update, which earlier analysis expected, is not scheduled. I put the probability of new 2030 targets above the street's estimates inside 18 months at 25 percent.

So what: the expectation gap is unfavourable for the brokers' models but favourable for the share price. The share price already discounts the cuts: the stock de-rated to its five-year low while FY2027 consensus EPS fell only 3 percent in twelve months.

Counter-case. The strongest counter-case is that the market is less prepared for the cuts than I think. The ratings base (69 percent Buy, no Sells) and target prices (mean €168, 48 percent above the price) have little room to become more bullish and plenty of room to become less so. One or two downgrades on a light February guide could take the shares below €102, the price at a trough multiple on unchanged earnings, before the July proofs. What would change my view: the order signed with its value disclosed before 24 February (February then becomes the upgrade event), or NKT's Q3 on 19 November showing softer award prices or down-payment terms (the contract-vintage story would then weaken for all three leaders).

Versus the market. The market's central path is "beat and raise in February"; mine is "meet, guide light, cut EPS and cash, raise in July". The difference between the two paths is worth about 10 percent of the share price between February and July, in either direction.

Conclusion: The next six months bring estimate cuts (EPS 3 to 6 percent, FY2027 cash 15 to 25 percent) and a light FY2027 guide rather than upgrades. The upgrade scope sits in July 2027 and depends on the order and the Transmission margin, so the narrative must pass through a cut-and-absorb phase before it can broaden.

Score: 36, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is likely first set 2-4% below the EUR 936m FY2027 consensus in February (65-70%) and only then raised by EUR 20-40m in July (45-50%), while consensus EPS is likely cut 3-6% and FY2027 cash 15-25% in February and only partly restored in July. Against revenue growth of about 6-8%, the net expected revision over 6-12 months is mildly negative (about -0.2 to -0.4 times growth), with the narrative passing through cut-and-absorb before it can broaden. Coherent with the fourth-set group's 35; above TT Electronics because a July raise is better than even.

8Current momentum: guidance, sell-side, narrative, technicals, and the same for peers

Every element of Nexans's own momentum is against the stock today.

  • Guidance momentum: none. Nexans has made one acquisition-led raise (July 2026) and one confirmation (October 2026), and no guidance event is available before 24 February.
  • Sell-side momentum: rolling over. The dashboard pins a B (as at 23 October), but the underlying series has turned. FY2027 consensus EPS is -3 percent over one month and -1 percent over three months (still +5 percent over six); FY2027 EBITDA is flat over one month and +3 percent over three; target prices are -2 percent over one month and flat over three, after +21 percent over six months. The share of Buy ratings rose 22 points to 69 percent over three months (Jefferies upgraded to Buy on 11 October, citing the 30 percent discount to peers), and the revision-momentum score is 1.
  • Narrative momentum: negative since 22 October. The shares fell about 7 percent in two days on a sales beat, because the order was absent and no profit data was given.
  • Technical momentum: D. The price is 16 percent below its 200-day moving average (€135.65; the 50-day average is €134.41), relative strength is at the 18th percentile of the universe, and the price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range of €107.73 to €165.96. The one positive technical sign is that the 200-day average has risen in each of the last twelve months.

Peers are in a down-phase on price and an up-phase on estimates. Technical momentum is D or F across the cable and electrification group, and earnings momentum is A at six of the peers (table below). Prysmian's Q3 on 29 October was a beat and its third guidance raise of 2026: the FY2026 EBITDA midpoint rose 9 percent to €3.1bn; the Transmission margin was 20.0 percent against 17.8 percent a year earlier, though below 21.2 percent in Q2 and Bernstein's 20.9 percent; the Industrial and Construction margin reached a record 17.6 percent on data-centre demand; and the backlog stood at €16.5bn plus €2bn awarded. Prysmian's shares rose only 2 percent (Bernstein called the results "well understood"), and Deutsche Bank cut its target price to €163 from €167 on the sector's de-rating while raising its estimates by 6 to 8 percent.

Elsewhere, NKT raised its guidance to €400m to €430m with a 20.2 percent Transmission margin and reports Q3 on 19 November; Cenergy raised to €390m to €420m; and Rexel raised twice on North American data-centre demand (same-day sales +11.4 percent), with Europe +4.5 percent.

Peer valuations have split, and Nexans has become a sector proxy. On their own ten-year P/E percentiles, peers range from Pfisterer at the 0th to Siemens at the 98th; Nexans is at the 22nd, and at the 5th of five years. Nexans's six-month co-movement with the large-capitalisation electrification complex is the highest in two years (R-squared 57 percent, beta 1.03, closest to ABB, Prysmian and NKT).

Inference: Nexans's momentum is the mirror image of a setup Richard likes. Estimates and guidance are flat to down at Nexans and up at peers; prices are down everywhere; and the group's multiple is contracting while its earnings rise (Bernstein: "peer earnings upgrades have consistently supported positive consensus revisions while sector multiples contracted"). Nexans has become a sector proxy precisely because its own news has gone quiet. Its share price over the next three months will be set by Siemens Energy's targets (11 November), NKT's Q3 (19 November), the interest-rate and artificial-intelligence-financing regime, and French politics, none of which the company controls.

So what: an investor buying now is buying ahead of the proofs, not on them. No momentum element favours the stock today, which is consistent with the Bottoming phase and with the dashboard's pinned letters (technical D, thematic D).

Counter-case. The counter-case is that peer estimate momentum (A across the group) is the leading indicator, and Nexans's own revisions follow in July. Prysmian and NKT executing the same 2023 to 2026 price regime at 20 percent Transmission margins is the best external evidence that Nexans's contract-vintage effect is real. What would change my view: Nexans's relative-strength percentile above 50 with the 50-day average turning up, or a single broker raising its FY2027 EBITDA estimate on the order's signature.

Versus the market. The dashboard's pinned B for sell-side momentum is a lagging reading. The one- and three-month series say that sell-side momentum has gone, and I would describe Nexans's revision momentum as negative into February.

Conclusion: Momentum is against the stock on every count (revisions rolling over, no guidance event until February, a D technical rating at the 18th relative-strength percentile), while peers show rising estimates and falling multiples. The case therefore rests on proofs still ahead and on a sector regime the company cannot influence.

Score: 32, set by the Rater. One measure barely positive and one in the bottom fifth would give C, but I move it one step to D because the parts strongly contradict the positive one: the revision-momentum score has fallen from 7 to 1, the three-month EPS revision is -2% (28th percentile), guidance has had only an acquisition-led raise and no event before February, the narrative turned negative on 22 October and the price is 16% below its 200-day average near the 52-week low. Peers' rising estimates (A across the group) lift it a little within the band but cannot pull it up on their own.

9Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

The case is simple in its drivers and complicated below EBITDA. Three drivers generate about four-fifths of the FY2025 to FY2028 EBITDA increase: Transmission conversion, Republic Wire and Grid capacity. Each depends on something different that does not fail with the others: signed contracts and a delivered vessel; US building-wire prices; and European utility frameworks and commissioning dates. Three dated checks cover about 80 percent of the uncertainty in FY2027: the order's signature by April 2027; the H2 2026 Transmission margin and the FY2027 guide on 24 February; and Republic Wire's first disclosed half-year and US price announcements. Grid needs only the quarterly print. The operating case is therefore tractable to monitor.

The complication lies below EBITDA and in cash. Four EPS bases, three cash definitions, IFRS 5 restatements and a FactSet half-year data artefact (which put the model 13 percent short of the Analyst's EPS until it was corrected) make the market's own arithmetic on Nexans unusually error-prone. The company gives no guidance on EPS, depreciation, interest or tax, and its cash target uses a basis most brokers do not model.

The 18-month range of outcomes widens sharply from EBITDA to EPS to cash.

  • FY2027 adjusted EBITDA: about ±6 percent. 80 percent of the probability lies between €860m and €960m around €909m, with 15 percent below that range and 5 percent above; the expected value is about €900m.
  • FY2027 EPS: about ±10 percent (€7.1 to €8.75 on the Analyst's basis), because depreciation (€290m to €320m), the tax rate (29 to 32 percent) and the hedging line add their own uncertainty.
  • FY2027 free cash flow: about ±30 percent (€180m to €330m), because working capital on a flat backlog is the least predictable line: a single large award, or its absence, moves it by €50m to €100m.

FY2026 is about 85 percent known. In relative terms the range is widest in H1 2027, which carries the order's timing, the first full half-year of higher energy costs, Grid start-up costs and five months of Republic Wire scope under a possibly changed tariff regime.

Seven assumptions must hold for the base case.

  1. The replacement order is signed by end-March 2027 and loads Halden to mid-2028.
  2. Legacy Transmission frameworks finish by late 2026 (Bernstein's view, already visible in H1 2026).
  3. Grid capacity is commissioned on schedule, with start-up costs absorbed inside a 16 percent margin.
  4. US building-wire spreads hold near 15 percent, although the Section 232 tariff schedule on refined copper (15 percent from January 2027, 30 percent from 2028) is itself in doubt, with over 600,000 tonnes of copper in COMEX stocks.
  5. Connect's European margin stays above 11 percent without a construction recovery.
  6. No execution incident occurs on a 525 kV project in its first industrial production.
  7. The single-source supply of Borealis cable compound holds, and the roll-off of the 18-month energy hedge through 2027 stays within the model.

The sudden, large risks sit in high-voltage execution and utilisation, and this company's crises have arrived in clusters. In 2013 Nexans issued two profit warnings and followed them with a 42 percent rights issue; in 2018 operating income fell 31 percent on a 21 percent organic fall in high-voltage sales. In those episodes the bears were right in the short term about 80 percent of the time, and the shares fell 30 to 50 percent. The sector's equivalents are Prysmian's Western Link (€165m of provisions and a 38 percent share-price fall, followed by a 412 percent rise over seven years) and NKT's Solutions EBITDA falling from €63m to €14m in 2019.

Today's conditions share one feature with those episodes and lack the others. The shared feature is a specialised production line that could be under-utilised. The missing features are a thin backlog, a complex portfolio and an aggressive guide: Nexans now has a 4.5-year backlog with 10 to 15 percent down-payments and cost recovery on cancellation, a simpler portfolio and a conservative guide. The table below gives my probability and size for each sudden risk; the risk that breaks the case is the correlated cluster.

Perception risks are widespread but partly spent.

  • Peer read-across: NKT's Q3 on 19 November, and NKT's Karlskrona ramp from Q2 2027 as a sector execution test.
  • The capacity-overhang narrative: each data point on a new entrant de-rates the group years before prices move.
  • Artificial-intelligence financing: the credit spreads of "neocloud" data-centre operators are widening.
  • Interest rates and French sovereign risk into the 2027 election.
  • The copper "false friend": a fall in the copper price would reverse the €75m H1 2026 gain on Core exposure metal in reported profit, while releasing working capital.

The Norwegian krone works against intuition: a 10 percent fall in the krone adds €28m to €32m of net income and takes about €140m off equity.

Nexans is a medium-cyclicality business. About 40 percent of EBITDA (Connect) follows construction and distributor stock cycles; Grid is regulated and framework-backed; and Transmission is backed by its backlog to 2028 and exposed to the capacity cycle after that. Historically, the market marks a cable maker down when new capacity is announced, one to two quarters before earnings fall, and trough multiples arrive with execution failures rather than with demand failures.

The downside to a fair trough multiple is about 10 percent on unchanged earnings, against about 23 percent upside on delivery: roughly 2.5 to 1. At the ten-year 10th-percentile multiple of 9.5x, unchanged earnings give about €102 a share (-10 percent). A plausible 10 percent earnings cut at 9.5x gives about €92 (-19 percent; Jefferies's May bear case was €97). Only a 2013- or 2018-style cluster (earnings -20 percent at 8.5x) takes the price to about €73 (-36 percent). Against these, FY2027 delivery at the ten-year median multiple gives about €140.

Five judgements move the shares most. No single operating judgement moves FY2027 EPS by more than 5 percent, but one turn of the multiple outweighs them all. The table uses the model's basis: each €10m of EBITDA is about €0.16 of EPS after 30 percent tax on 43.7m shares, and FY2027 EPS is €8.38.

Grid's skew is upward, because consensus already sits €7m below the model. And with a beta of about 1.0 and an R-squared of 57 percent to the electrification complex, a 10 percent move in the sector means about a 10 percent move in Nexans's shares, whatever the company reports.

Counter-case. The strongest counter-case to "predictable at EBITDA" is the disclosure gap: Nexans gives nothing on profit, margin or cash until 24 February, and it chose not to comment on either the order or the H2 margin on a day its shares fell 7 percent. What would raise my view of the risk: no order by end-April 2027; a FY2027 guide midpoint below €880m; a Connect margin below 11 percent in H2 2026. What would lower it: the order signed with its value and loading profile disclosed; an H2 2026 Transmission margin at or above 15 percent; a FY2027 cash range with a midpoint above €300m on the company's basis.

Versus the market. The market prices Nexans as riskier than its EBITDA range implies: a 30 percent discount to peers and the 5th percentile of its five-year multiple range. The brokers model it as less risky than its EPS and cash ranges imply: their FY2027 EPS estimates run from €7.72 to €11.78, a spread four times wider than their EBITDA range, with the median near the top of what the accounts support. Both views are partly right, and February's accounts will resolve them.

Conclusion: The case is simple in its drivers and tractable to monitor, with an EBITDA range of about ±6 percent for FY2027. But it carries one dated binary item, wide EPS and cash ranges that the company does nothing to narrow, a history of clustered execution crises in exactly this part of the business, and a sector beta of one. Nexans is therefore a medium-risk case, with a positive skew against the share price and a negative skew against consensus.

Score: 56, set by the Rater. The memo's FY2027 EPS range is about +/-10% (EUR 7.1-8.75) around an EBITDA range of +/-6%, with three independent and trackable drivers and low fixed-rate leverage. But cash is +/-30%, the replacement order is a dated binary on timing (35% after March, under 10% lost), the company has a history of clustered high-voltage execution crises, Connect is cyclical, and the share price follows the sector with a beta of 1.0 and an R-squared of 57%. Coherent with the Risks groups at 56-58; above NKT, whose case is more concentrated on high-voltage execution, and below Banca Generali.

10Where the stock is in its lifecycle

The dashboard's rule puts the stock in the Bottoming phase, and the evidence supports that reading.

  • Price: near the 52-week low and 16 percent below the 200-day average; relative strength at the 18th percentile.
  • Revisions: the revision-momentum score has rolled from 7 to 1, with FY2027 EPS -3 percent over a month.
  • Valuation: the two-year-forward multiple is at the 5th percentile of five years on consensus EPS.
  • Sentiment: poor, although ratings remain bullish (69 percent Buy).
  • The stock-specific part of the fall: largely spent, with about 10 percent downside to a trough multiple on unchanged earnings.
  • The sector: in a down-phase on price and an up-phase on estimates.
  • News flow and the thesis: company news is quiet until 24 February, and the thesis is not yet broadening, because the proofs (the order, the Transmission margin print, the cash print and the new team's first full year) are still ahead.

Inference: Nexans is Bottoming, not yet turning up. The stock has completed the de-rating part of a bottom: half of its six-month fall was stock-specific, on identifiable items that can be resolved. It has not completed the estimate-reset part: consensus EPS and cash estimates still sit above what the accounts will show, and the first FY2027 guide will probably be light. The turn up needs three things in sequence (figure below).

I put the probability that the stock is turning up by the July 2027 results at 55 to 60 percent; still bottoming, with the proofs delayed but intact, at 25 to 30 percent; and collapsing at about 10 to 15 percent. A collapse would follow a lost order, an execution incident, or a sector de-rating on capacity or interest rates that the stock follows with a beta of one. The catalysts that would broaden the thesis (superconducting data-centre awards, a Great Sea Interconnector restart, a pivot to returning capital) belong to 2028.

So what: build a position across the February event rather than before it. For a Bottoming stock, buying ahead of the proofs is right only if two conditions hold: the downside to the trough multiple is acceptable (about 10 percent on unchanged earnings, about 20 percent on an earnings cut), and the upside to the median multiple on delivery is a multiple of that downside (about 25 percent plus dividends). On this memo's numbers both conditions hold. But the sequence argues for building the position across February rather than before it, because 24 February is more likely to be a cut-and-absorb day than a proof day.

Counter-case. The strongest counter-case is that the sector's estimate momentum pulls Nexans's multiple up before its own proofs arrive, as NKT and Prysmian re-rated on confirmation rather than surprise in 2026; in that case, waiting for February costs the first leg of the rise. What would change my view: the order signed before February (which brings the turn forward), or NKT's Q3 showing the contract-vintage effect fading (which pushes it back).

Versus the market. Jefferies's "compelling entry point" and Bernstein's "near-term risk-reward skews negative" both describe the Bottoming phase, from opposite ends. I side with Bernstein on the next event and with Jefferies on the next year.

Conclusion: The stock is Bottoming: the de-rating is largely done and the estimate reset is not. The turn up is most likely in July 2027 (55 to 60 percent), and the February 2027 results are the event that decides whether the bottom holds.

Score: 52, set by the Rater. The memo's Bottoming is right and the computed Reinforcing is wrong: the de-rating is done (price near its 52-week low, 16% below the 200-day average, relative strength at the 18th percentile) but the estimate reset is not, so February 2027 is more likely a cut-and-absorb event and the turn is dated to July 2027 (55-60%), with collapse at 10-15%. Contracted earnings growth behind the bottom puts it above a plain stalling case, but it is less advanced than Greggs' early Turning.

11The fair multiple

Viewforth's guideline sets the fair multiple at 11.05x for the Bottoming phase; the model summary's 15.82x is inconsistent with that guideline, so I treat 15.82x as the bull case. The guideline derives the fair multiple from the stock's phase and from its own ten-year range of two-year-forward P/E: 10th percentile 9.5x, 35th 11.4x, median 12.3x, 75th 14.0x and 90th 15.8x. The Phases page of 4 November 2026 gives the starting phase as Bottoming and the guideline fair multiple as 11.05x, the 30th percentile and 12 percent below the multiple that page reads today (12.58x). The model's one-page summary computed its return at 15.82x, the 90th-percentile "mania" band, which the guideline reserves for peak-delivery phases. I therefore treat 11.05x as the guideline of record and 15.82x as a bull case; section 12 reports both.

Today's multiple has three readings, and the difference matters. On FactSet consensus two-year-forward EPS (€10.79) the stock is at 10.4x, the 5th percentile of five years and the 22nd of ten. On the model's EPS, the model summary reads 12.2x and the Phases page 12.6x. The ten-year history of the multiple is built on consensus EPS, so the like-for-like reading is 10.4x against a 12.3x median. But consensus EPS is 5 to 8 percent too high for the February accounts, so after the cuts the same price reads about 11x on the consensus basis, the 25th to 35th percentile.

Conversely, the model's EPS basis runs 6 to 9 percent below the brokers' basis, because it deducts acquired-intangible amortisation and uses diluted shares and a 30 percent tax rate. Applying a percentile multiple from the consensus history to the model's EPS is therefore conservative by about that amount. Two practical consequences follow: about half of the apparent 18 percent discount to the median closes through estimate cuts rather than price rises, and the model's return at any given multiple carries a 6 to 9 percent basis cushion.

My fair multiple is 12.3x, the ten-year median, for a 12- to 18-month horizon, conditional on the February and July 2027 proofs. 11.05x is the right floor today for a Bottoming stock whose estimates are still falling; 14.0x (the 75th percentile) requires the proofs plus a sector recovery; and 15.8x is not available to this company in this cycle.

A premium to the median is not justified. A premium would need either a long runway for high-return reinvestment or proof that Transmission returns survive 2029, and Nexans has neither. Capex of 5 to 6 percent of sales earns high returns, but acquisitions earn lower ones; the model plateaus the Transmission margin at 16.5 percent; and Nexans is the weakest of the three high-voltage leaders.

A discount to the median is not justified once proof arrives. EPS grows about 20 percent a year in FY2027 and FY2028 on contracted drivers, ROCE recovers towards 19 percent, the balance sheet deleverages to 0.5x without deals, and the company has met or beaten its initial guidance every year since 2022.

Peers point to the same answer from the other side. NKT trades at 14.8x and Prysmian at 13.9x current P/E, with 75 and 25 percent of their EBITDA respectively in high voltage, against 28 percent for Nexans. A sum-of-the-parts valuation (Jefferies values Nexans at 8x consolidated EBITDA, against 14x for Prysmian's transmission business) also lands at a stock-specific median rather than at peers' multiples. The industry drives the multiple's path over 18 months (57 percent of daily variance), while the company drives its level (the 30 percent discount, resolvable on proof); that is why I express the fair multiple as a range with a conditional centre rather than as a point.

Counter-case. The case for a higher fair multiple is that conservative guiders who beat and raise tend to compound their multiples: if July 2027 starts an organic raise cycle, the stock could reach the 75th percentile inside 18 months, as NKT did. The case for a lower one is the 2018 precedent of 8.0x at the trough, if Halden stands idle. What would change my view: an organic raise in July 2027 (towards 14x), or no order by April 2027 (towards 11x and below).

Versus the market. The sell-side's target prices (mean €168, median €172.50) imply about 15.5x to 16x two-year-forward consensus EPS, close to the model summary's 15.82x. I think that is a peak-delivery multiple applied to a Bottoming stock whose estimates are still falling, and the market's own pricing (a 5th-percentile multiple) disagrees with the sell-side's targets.

Conclusion: The guideline fair multiple for the Bottoming phase is 11.05x, and the model's 15.82x is a peak-delivery multiple that overstates the base case. My fair multiple is the ten-year median of 12.3x, earned on the February and July 2027 proofs, with 11.05x as the floor and 14.0x as the stretch.

Score: 62, set by the Rater. Neutral on both gives C. Placed in the upper half because both readings lean cheap and the pure-electrification perimeter with contracted growth to 2028 deserves at least the 12.3x median once proven; held down because the consensus EPS behind the multiple is 5-10% too high (after the cuts the same price reads about 11x, still neutral) and part of the peer discount is structural (scale, backlog, no optical fibre).

12Total shareholder return, Dupont framework

How the return is calculated. Value per share at each horizon is the two-year-forward EPS at that date multiplied by the fair multiple, plus the dividends received. The 14-month horizon (31 December 2027) uses FY2029 EPS of €10.84 and dividends of €6.50 (€3.10 and €3.40). The 32-month horizon (30 June 2029) uses about €11.78, the model's extrapolation beyond FY2030's €11.56, and dividends of €10.25 (adding €3.75). The starting two-year-forward EPS is about €9.31, at 12.2x. Earnings and the multiple combine multiplicatively, and dividends add.
